opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of that debate comes down to how you define "novel." People sometimes picture a creative genius producing an idea from nothing, but that's not really how human creativity works either. Most new ideas are recombinations: you take something from one area, notice it fits a problem in another, and suddenly you have something nobody has done before. The Transformer itself wasn't magic. It pulled together attention, some engineering tricks, and a willingness to throw out recurrence, and the combination turned out to be powerful.

So when people say a model is "just predicting the next token" and therefore can't be original, I don't find that persuasive. To predict the next token really well across everything humans have written, you have to build a pretty rich internal model of the world, and once you have that, you can explore combinations nobody has written down yet. We already see models produce proofs, code, and approaches that aren't in their training data in any literal sense.

Where I think the skeptics have a point is on the loop around the idea. Generating a candidate idea is one thing. Knowing which of a thousand candidates is good, testing it, getting feedback from reality, and iterating is where much of real research happens. Models are getting better at that too, especially as we give them more compute at inference time and let them run experiments and check their own work. As that loop tightens, I expect the "can AI be truly creative" question to start feeling a bit old-fashioned. We'll just be looking at the results.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention or challenge Yann LeCun to prove he generated a completely novel idea.

r002.rationale: It suggests the debate may become old-fashioned as models improve, but does not clearly prioritize building AI over debating the question.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the debate is a little bit confused about what "novel" means. If you look at how humans come up with new ideas, almost all of it is recombination. You take two things you already know and you notice they fit together in a way nobody pointed out before. Attention was like that. Mixture of experts was like that. None of the pieces were new; the arrangement was. So when people say a model can only remix its training data, my reaction is, well, yes, and so do we.

The thing people are really asking, I think, is whether a model can get to the frontier, where the answer isn't anywhere in the data at all. And my honest view is that the hard part there isn't generating the idea. Generating candidate ideas is cheap. Humans have terrible ideas all day long. The hard part is the filter: knowing which of your hundred ideas is the one worth spending six months on. That's taste, and taste comes from having tried things and been wrong. Right now the models are very good at the generation half and still pretty weak at the filtering half, mostly because they don't get to run the experiment and feel the pain when it fails.

So I don't think there's some magic ingredient humans have that machines are missing. I think there's a feedback loop humans have that machines are only starting to get. Once a model can propose something, test it, see that it didn't work, and update, I'd expect it to produce things we'd all agree are new. It'll be messy and most of what it tries won't work, but that's what research looks like for us too.

r002.rationale: It discusses the debate and describes a feedback loop models need, but does not prioritize building AI over debating novelty.

astra-6.text:
I think people sometimes set a higher bar for AI than they do for humans. If a person has a new idea, we don’t require that it have no connection to anything they’ve ever learned. Most ideas come from combining things you know, noticing a pattern, or trying something and seeing whether it works. I don’t see why AI couldn’t do those things.

And novelty by itself is pretty easy. You can generate something random that nobody’s ever said before. The interesting question is whether you can generate an idea that’s both new and useful. Can you find a better solution to a problem? Can you make a prediction that turns out to be right? That seems like something we can test, rather than a philosophical distinction we need to settle in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people sometimes set a much higher bar for AI than they do for humans. When a person has a new idea, it’s usually some combination of things they’ve learned, plus a lot of searching and trying things. It’s not coming out of nowhere. So I don’t see why a machine couldn’t do that, too.

The interesting question is whether it can come up with something that we didn’t know before and that turns out to be useful or true. You can test that. If it proposes an experiment or a mathematical argument, does it work? That seems more productive than arguing about whether the idea is “completely novel.”
